To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

both the cytochrome P450 and the flavoprotein monooxygenase catalyze N-hydroxylation of 2-aminobenzene, and that the nonenzymes reaction of N-hydroxysubstrate with DNA may be a significant source of in vivo carcinogen-DNA binding.

both the cytochrome P450 and the flavoprotein monooxygenase catalyze the formation of the carcinogenic N-hydroxy metabolite of 2-aminfluorene, and that this reactive metabolite reacts directly with DNA to form covalently bound products.

both cytochrome-P450 and the flavoprotein monooxygenase catalyzed the N-hydroxylation of AF and that the N-hydroxymetabolite formed by either enzyme was capable of reacting with DNA to form covalent adduct(s).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolic formation and covalent binding of N-hydroxymethyl-2-aminobenzene (N-OH-MeAF), a proximate carcinogenic metabolite of 2-aminobiphenyl (2AB), to DNA.
the metabolic formation of carcinogens from precarcinogens.
the metabolic activation of the carcinogen AF.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both cytochrome-P450 and the flavoprotein monooxygenase are involved in the metabolic activation of AF to N-OH-Af.

both the cytochrome P450 and flavin-containing mono-oxygenases are involved in the metabolic formation of the carcinogenic N-hydroxy metabolite of 2-aminfluorene, but the relative contribution of each enzyme to the total metabolic N-hydroxylation of this carcinogen is not clear.
the metabolic N-oxidations of AF are catalyzed by both the cytochrome P450- and flavoprotein monooxygenase-dependent pathways.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the formation of N-OHF by cytochrome P450 and flavin-containing monoxygenase, and subsequent covalent binding of N-OHF to DNA, is species specific.
the formation of N-OHF by both the cytochrome P450 and FMO is a major metabolic pathway for AF in the species examined.
N-oxidation is an important pathway in the metabolic activation of AF, but the reaction of N-OHAF with DNA is relatively inefficient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic formation of the proximate carcinogen, N-hydroxy-AF, is catalyzed by both the flavin-containing and cytochrome P450 monooxygenases.

the flavin-containing monoxygenase and cytochrome P450 enzymes are both capable of N-oxidizing 2-aminouorene to N-hydroxy-AF, but that the flavin monooxygenase is a much more efficient N-oxidizer of 2-aminuorene than cytochrome P45O.

N-hydroxylation of 2-aminfluorene (2-AF) occurs in the liver of a variety of species, including humans, and that this reaction is catalyzed by both cytochrome p450 and flavin-containing mono-oxygenase (FMO).
